stories.topic: A father's gift and three lifetime regrets
stories.summary: Asked what he would have pursued no matter what, Ajay says he can't picture himself outside the path his father set. His father gave him an interest in the world and died when Ajay was seventeen. With that interest in place, Ajay says, he never needed money, books or universities. He would have powered through anyway. He then names three great lifetime regrets: never learning a musical instrument, never seriously knowing maths, and not knowing more biology.
stories.insight: Deep curiosity is often inherited as a disposition rather than chosen as a goal. Even a restless polymath carries a short list of roads not taken. Later in the episode, Nomsita turns the first regret into a recommendation for viewers.
stories.quote: I have three great regrets in my life. I don't know how to play a musical instrument. I wish I knew maths, as in like really seriously know maths. And I wish I knew more biology.

stories.topic: The introvert who hated his face on camera
stories.summary: Amit calls himself an extreme introvert who doesn't find it easy to put himself out there, yet he started his audio podcast anyway. When EIE moved to YouTube, neither host knew anything about the medium. Amit hated how he looked in the early episodes and wished the camera sat higher to hide his double chin. He kept going. Now, nearing episode 100, Ajay says he is 'astonished and happy beyond my wildest dreams' that YouTube's democratisation lets them make timeless material without needing a BBC commission.
stories.insight: Comfort in your own skin comes from doing the uncomfortable thing again and again. It is not something you need before you start.
stories.quote: But I just barreled through because I'm like fine, I gotta, A, I gotta get comfortable in my skin, whatever my skin is. And B, you know, comfort zone is not a good place.

stories.topic: The early-morning panic before 'Rules, Not Discretion'
stories.summary: Before recording the EIE episode on rules versus discretion, Ajay woke up in a panic. The paper behind that episode had been one of the great highs of his life as a PhD student, a long time ago. What if he had missed something essential in the years since? He hadn't, but he values having had the panic.
stories.insight: Even on your home turf, keep a live sense of what you might not know. That nervousness is what stops expertise from turning into smug confidence.
stories.quote: So I had a brief panic like could it be that I have missed something essential? It was not the case, but I did have that panic. So it's you know it's good to be skeptical, it's good to be nervous about what you don't know.

stories.summary: A friend was torn between several book ideas. Amit asked him one question: if you had only one book in you, and you would die once it was done, which book would you write? The friend named something deeply personal. Amit told him that was the book to write. The friend went on to write something else.
stories.insight: A forced-choice question can quickly reveal what matters most to you. Acting on the answer is the hard part.
stories.quote: You have one book in you. You will die when that book is done. What book are you gonna write?

stories.topic: The poker grinders who wouldn't get up to pee
stories.summary: Nomsita asked how young people should read pop culture's image of greatness as sleepless, protein-bar-fuelled grind. In reply, Amit recalls his professional poker days. Some players multi-tabled fifteen tables at once and kept a bottle beside them so they never had to leave the screen to use the bathroom.
stories.insight: Hard work matters, but treating self-punishing grind as the only route to excellence is a distortion. Ideas also need slow, quiet time to marinate.
stories.quote: there were guys who would be multi-tabling fifteen tables at a time, and they'd actually keep a bottle with them because they wouldn't want to get up to go pee. And I think that kind of thing is just crazy.

stories.topic: Newton and the moon that didn't add up
stories.summary: Newton already had pretty much all the right ideas when he did a rough calculation of the moon's period. It came out ten to fifteen percent off. He concluded he was wrong and sat quietly with it. Months and years later, better constants reached him, the pieces clicked, and he realised he had been right all along.
stories.insight: Greatness looks less like a frantic sprint and more like extreme concentration plus a perfectionist's refusal to accept a near-miss. Hence Ajay's line: don't fetishise the sprint.
stories.quote: And Newton concluded, Okay, so I'm wrong. And he sat quietly. And then some months and years later, some better constants came to him, and then the pieces of the puzzle clicked. And he said, Ah, I was right all along.

stories.summary: On an earlier shoot at the same location, Amit skipped the crew's usual ten-to-fifteen-minute neighbourhood walk. His chest felt constricted and something seemed wrong. This was before the heart attack discussed in 'The Heart of Disruption'. Now he can do the walk again. He adds that even a blocked nostril during a cold makes him realise he should have been grateful for every day he could breathe freely.
stories.insight: This is Brene Brown's point made personal: we chase the extraordinary, then beg for a normal moment once it's gone. Ordinary health is worth noticing while you have it.
stories.quote: So you know, and now it's not there. Now I can come on the walk. That ordinary moment is so important.

stories.topic: Gukesh's world-championship team had no Indian quota
stories.summary: Responding to Paul Graham's point that most of the world's best people are born abroad, Ajay cites Gukesh's world-championship campaign. Anand helped him bring in a Polish helper and a bunch of others, building an unabashedly international team with just one Indian. To win a world championship, you need a team at the top of world capabilities.
stories.insight: The same logic applies to Indian firms. Not all the knowledge is in India, and a culturally homogeneous workplace is an impediment, because diverse teams have better debates.
stories.quote: It was a unabashedly international team. There was no Indian quota.

stories.topic: Being turned into someone's bug tester
stories.summary: With young colleagues, Ajay is happy to point out a type of mistake once, twice, even three times. When the same error comes back a fifth or sixth time, he realises the person is only fixing whatever he flags, like a typist correcting a typo. They never extract the general principle. The skilled senior has been reduced to a clerical bug tester.
stories.insight: Promise doesn't show in the absence of errors. It shows in a thirst for excellence: shipping your genuine best, and asking after each correction what deeper rule you missed.
stories.quote: Whereas a mechanical approach of just implementing corrections, then you have turned your skilled master into your bug tester, which is a waste of life.

stories.topic: The king of typos and his reader copy-editors
stories.summary: Across hundreds of columns and many thousands of blog posts, Amit has accepted that he will never catch every typo. His system now is to write, read it over once, read it over twice, and publish. A typo always slips through. Within a couple of days, readers write in to point it out, and the page is clean.
stories.insight: Shipping and letting the world help you fix things beats endless private polishing. It is a working example of 'perfection is the enemy of production'.
stories.quote: And I will always miss a typo. But always, always, always. Within a couple of days no typos exist on that page because readers have written to me

stories.topic: FU money, FO money, and the danger of comfort
stories.summary: Amit recalls asking Roshan Abbas on The Seen and the Unseen about FU money and FO money. Roshan said he had FU money but not FO money, and gave figures for both that Amit found insane. Amit says he is far from both, but he is comfortable, and that comfort worries him.
stories.insight: Complacency is a side effect of prosperity. Once you're comfortable, the hunger that drove you can quietly fade unless you keep pushing yourself.
stories.quote: I'm far from both of them. But I'm comfortable. And that comfort kinda worries me.

recommendations.creator: Cal Newport
recommendations.context: Came up in Amit's answer to Nomsita's question about pop culture equating greatness with sleepless grind. Amit read it on a flight; it is Newport's book after Deep Work.
recommendations.reason: It argues you don't need a constant mad sprint. You can live a quiet life and let ideas marinate, and creativity emerges from that over time. A counterweight to hustle culture.

recommendations.creator: Luke Burgis
recommendations.context: Amit's source for the terms thin desires and thick desires. Burgis studied René Girard, who coined the term mimetic desire.
recommendations.reason: It helps you tell desires copied from others (wanting the Mercedes, the prize, the label) from what you intrinsically want. Only the latter makes you put in the hard yards.

recommendations.creator: Oliver Burkeman
recommendations.context: Mentioned (Amit half-remembers the title) alongside Gurwinder Bhogal's tweet that your future is constantly shrinking.
recommendations.reason: It makes you reckon with how little time a life actually holds, which works as a spur to act now rather than keep preparing.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons (Scorsese's segment of New York Stories)
recommendations.creator: Martin Scorsese
recommendations.context: Part of the late-1980s anthology New York Stories, with shorts by Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola and Woody Allen. Amit first saw it when his father was administrative director of the film institute in Pune.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Scorsese's short a masterpiece whose scenes still play in his head. It inspired the name of their course. It is also where he first heard Procol Harum's 'A Whiter Shade of Pale', over a slow-motion shot of a falling cigarette: 'the magic of film editing'. Even many Scorsese fans have missed it.

recommendations.creator: Martin Scorsese
recommendations.context: Recommended after Nomsita's Scorsese pick reminded him of it.
recommendations.reason: In the late 1970s The Band, often Dylan's backing band on tour, decided to retire after one last concert and invited friends to perform, including Dylan and Van Morrison (Amit's favourite). Scorsese filmed it. Amit calls it 'absolutely stirring stuff'.

recommendations.item: Roger Ebert's review of New York Stories
recommendations.creator: Roger Ebert
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as 'Roger Ebert's masterful review' of Scorsese's Life Lessons.
recommendations.reason: A companion read to the short film that named their course.

recommendations.item: Waking Life (and Richard Linklater's whole filmography)
recommendations.creator: Richard Linklater
recommendations.context: Vaishnav's first pick after Amit drafted the crew for recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Vaishnav feels Linklater captures the essence of life. His films taught Vaishnav how we look at people, how people look at us, and gave him a deeper self-awareness.

recommendations.context: Vaishnav's second recommendation: a practice, not a work.
recommendations.reason: Spend time with yourself and think about life. Watch yourself approach a problem 'just like a cat approaches a prey'.

recommendations.creator: Rockstar Games
recommendations.context: Vaishnav's third pick, a video game, after Amit insisted he give the why.
recommendations.reason: It is a slow, peaceful game with a thick story, history it gets right, thick characters, well-written dialogue and strong acting. It puts you among some twenty people running from the law and makes you decide what's right and wrong. Vaishnav cried at the end and learned from it.

recommendations.creator: Wim Wenders
recommendations.context: A film Amit, Vaishnav and Nomsita have long been pushing Ajay to watch.
recommendations.reason: It changed her view of life, of filmmaking and of work. She was struck by how it pairs the striving of just being at it with moments of silence and solitude we rarely get. The colour grade is beautiful.

recommendations.creator: Martin Scorsese
recommendations.context: A film about Bob Dylan and friends on tour.
recommendations.reason: It captures the hunger the hosts keep describing: to get to something, to do something, and to do it with the people you love.

recommendations.context: Nomsita turns Ajay's lifetime regret into a recommendation.
recommendations.reason: If you have even two percent of the willpower, do it. It changes your life and your mind, and can give you the concentration and meditation that are otherwise hard to find.

recommendations.creator: John Coltrane
recommendations.context: The opening Good Gyan, found on the Twitter account Melodies and Masterpieces: 'You can play a shoestring if you're sincere.'
recommendations.reason: Amit's answer to people who say they lack the gear or resources to pursue what they love.

recommendations.creator: Greg Isenberg
recommendations.context: A tweet offering five words that save fifty thousand: 'Greatness and comfort rarely coexist.'
recommendations.reason: It prompted a discussion of when to stay in your comfort zone and when to leave it.

recommendations.creator: Tiago Forte
recommendations.context: A tweet by 'the guy behind the second brain' listing four types of productivity: task, intellectual, emotional and social.
recommendations.reason: A corrective to treating productivity as nothing but ticking off tasks.

recommendations.item: Polina Pompliano quoting Brene Brown on normalcy
recommendations.creator: Brene Brown (via Polina Pompliano)
recommendations.context: The quote: we chase extraordinary moments instead of being grateful for ordinary ones, until hard things happen and all we beg for is a normal moment.
recommendations.reason: Amit finds it beautiful and lives it: a blocked nostril, or a walk he couldn't take before his heart attack, reminds him to value normalcy.

recommendations.creator: John Collison
recommendations.context: A screenshot of the Stripe co-founder's tweet, found via the Banger Archive account: 'The world is a museum of passion projects.'
recommendations.reason: It blew Amit's mind. Almost everything good around us exists because someone tenaciously made it happen. He urges viewers to follow such accounts.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Graham's 'very simple math' tweet: with five percent of world population and evenly distributed ability, 95% of the best at anything are born abroad.
recommendations.reason: A sharp answer to today's xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment.

recommendations.creator: Dharmesh
recommendations.context: The tweet: imperfectionists hit publish, ship product and iterate publicly; they dream big but iterate small.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it almost the mantra of his life, the same thing he tells his writing students.

recommendations.item: Rollo Tomassi quoting Ronnie Coleman on the hard yards
recommendations.creator: Ronnie Coleman (via Rollo Tomassi)
recommendations.context: The line: 'Everybody wants to be a bodybuilder, but nobody wants to lift no heavy ass weights.'
recommendations.reason: Aspiration means nothing without the work. Amit uses it to introduce thin versus thick desires.

recommendations.creator: Anthony Bourdain
recommendations.context: Bourdain's line about the guy in his head who wants to lie in bed, smoke pot and watch cartoons, and a life spent outwitting him. Amit couldn't relocate the original tweet.
recommendations.reason: It describes Amit's own daily struggle with the lazy self who wants to play online chess and binge YouTube.

recommendations.creator: Sahil Bloom
recommendations.context: A mini-essay titled 'There is no such thing as making it', built on the gazelle-and-lion parable.
recommendations.reason: It resonated as a warning against the complacency that prosperity breeds.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal on our shrinking future
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: The tweet: your future is constantly shrinking, so the longer you spend preparing for it, the smaller it will be.
recommendations.reason: Amit reads it as a call to action and calls Gurwinder a fount of wisdom.

recommendations.creator: Arnold Lobel (via the Frog and Toad Bot)
recommendations.context: An automated account that posts random quotes from Lobel's Frog and Toad books. This one: 'this is a cold grey day, but spring is just around the corner.'
recommendations.reason: A gentle reminder for anyone in dark times to zoom out, and to act.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The predecessor to this episode. Amit recalls its quote about letting the shore go to reach beyond the horizon, and Ajay recalls discussing the zero-to-one confidence index there.
recommendations.reason: More wisdom gathered from social media in the same format.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay refers to 'a ridiculous ten and a half hour conversation about my life' when explaining how his father shaped him.
recommendations.reason: The full story of the trajectory Ajay says he can't separate himself from.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The episode that triggered Ajay's early-morning panic about the paper he loved as a PhD student.
recommendations.reason: The deep dive behind the anecdote about staying sceptical of your own expertise.

recommendations.item: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (Episode 323, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah & Mohit Satyanand
recommendations.context: Plugged after Ajay used the SVB collapse to show how he could quickly catch up on financial regulation.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it explains a lot of the fundamentals and that he really enjoyed it.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The episode where Amit's heart attack was discussed, referenced in his story about the walk he couldn't take.
recommendations.reason: Background to his newfound gratitude for ordinary moments.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled for its line that people are brains, not stomachs.
recommendations.reason: It underpins the argument that wasting India's talent is a tragedy and growth is imperative.

recommendations.item: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Episode 8, EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited while arguing that high-skilled immigration is positive-sum, as in Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
recommendations.reason: It explains how concentrating the brightest people in one place creates a magnet for more talent.

recommendations.item: Luke Burgis Sees the Deer at His Window (Episode 337, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with Luke Burgis, where he first heard of thin and thick desires.
recommendations.reason: A fuller treatment of mimetic desire and why some wants are borrowed.

recommendations.item: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye & Roshan Abbas
recommendations.context: The episode where Roshan Abbas distinguished FU money from FO money.
recommendations.reason: The source of the anecdote behind Amit's worry about comfort and complacency.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay says the course constantly evangelises risk-taking. Amit reveals it is named after Scorsese's short film.
recommendations.reason: Aimed at people who work hard but don't take enough risks, which Ajay thinks describes many EIE viewers.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit repeatedly cites what he tells his writing students: perfection is the enemy of production, and use Grammarly, Hemingway or ChatGPT as a tool, not a crutch.
recommendations.reason: Where his bias-for-action approach to writing is taught.

core_ideas.concept: You can play a shoestring if you're sincere
core_ideas.explanation: Coltrane's line, used by Amit against the 'I lack resources' excuse: no Fender, no iPhone, no studio. Shakespeare found a quill. Ajay adds that you don't need an invitation to a Rockefeller castle in Italy or a hundred-dollar pen. You can read and think on the floor of an Indian second-class train.
core_ideas.quote: You can play a shoestring if you're sincere.

core_ideas.concept: Index every belief on a zero-to-one scale
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay tags everything he believes with how sure he is, and with whether it came from authorities or from his own first-principles reasoning. With this habit, entering a new field feels natural: everything starts near zero and you're used to operating amid ambiguity. It also guards against getting 'drunk on that smug nature of confidence'.
core_ideas.quote: It is always good to index your knowledge and your views on almost everything with like a zero to one scale of, you know, how sure am I.

core_ideas.concept: Be comfortable with physical discomfort
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that people wedded to a minimum level of luxury end up pushing away great experiences. Laugh at creature comforts, and accept dingy hotels, hard travel and bad food. Amit's caveat: real financial precarity imposes a cognitive burden, so learn to live frugally but don't romanticise worrying about rent.
core_ideas.quote: actually what is worth living for is a life of the mind, is a journey of the mind.

core_ideas.concept: Deep foundations make old fields portable
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay is a self-confessed novelty seeker who recklessly starts new fields. He isn't torn about leaving old ones, because once you deeply know a field's basic machinery, staying reasonably current is cheap. He hasn't tracked financial regulation for seven or eight years, including the post-SVB work on bank fragility under electronic payments, but a couple of papers would bring him up to speed.
core_ideas.quote: And so it's not difficult to stay up with old fields, so I don't feel like I'm letting anything go. I feel all those things are there in my pocket.

core_ideas.concept: Age trades horsepower for judgment
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay cites research suggesting memory, intelligence, problem-solving and even creativity peak in youth and middle age. Age brings judgment and integration: the spidey sense that a pawn storm is coming on the board. So play the violin, solve maths problems and play chess when young, and invest in breadth and strategy when older.
core_ideas.quote: What we get when we are older is different. What we get is judgment, what we get is integrative knowledge of putting a lot of things together.

core_ideas.concept: Greatness is visible only in hindsight; track your energy instead
core_ideas.explanation: Amit wonders whether greatness is a false target that may not coexist with happiness, and may arrive only by the way as you live (Annie Dillard). Ajay's practical answer: you can't see greatness while you're in the flow. The only observable signal is whether you are bringing full energy, interest and concentration to the work.
core_ideas.quote: So in the flow, the only thing that you know that is an observable input is the level of energy and excitement and concentration that you feel.

core_ideas.concept: Don't fetishise the sprint: you need both din and thehrav
core_ideas.explanation: You need the din of the world to collect dots, and stillness (thehrav, sukoon) to let them soak in. This echoes Cal Newport's Slow Productivity. Ajay adds that startup culture's adrenaline-laced sprint is not the model: Newton's and Einstein's were lives of quiet, extreme concentration and perfectionism.
core_ideas.quote: Because we make a picture of the world by joining dots, the more dots we have the more high definition our picture.

core_ideas.concept: Genius is a skin over the basics
core_ideas.explanation: A crew member asked whether imitating a Messi or a Coltrane makes sense. Amit's answer: you can't copy the style. Messi starts with love for the game, and love can also be an act of intentionality. Then he drills the basics daily, and his genius sits on top like a skin. Coltrane knew music theory inside out before the Coltrane style emerged.
core_ideas.quote: And then his genius is like a skin on top of that, right? And you can't copy just the skin.

core_ideas.concept: Productivity is more than tasks
core_ideas.explanation: Tiago Forte splits productivity into task (efficiency), intellectual (learning), emotional (well-being) and social (relationships), and warns against neglecting the last three. Ajay resists the word altogether: we are here to create things that didn't exist. Amit prefers 'intentionality'. We are intentional about tasks but rarely about what matters.
core_ideas.quote: you need a lot of task productivity, but ultimately you need imagination. Ultimately you need to come up with something new.

core_ideas.concept: Notice the ordinary: the 'last time' exercise
core_ideas.explanation: Brene Brown observes that we chase extraordinary moments until hardship makes us beg for a normal one. Ajay felt this when a broken ankle kept him in bed. A friend's exercise brings it alive: pause and imagine this is the last time you'll be with this person, or drink this hot chocolate. The moment changes colour.
core_ideas.quote: If only somebody could give you a postcard, uh drone delivered, that this is the last time you will do X.

core_ideas.concept: Be intentional, not calculating, in relationships
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay worries that intentionality in friendships sounds calculating. Amit's distinction is that caring effort isn't transactional. A friend of theirs has two practices: meeting a new person every week and spending real time with them, and calling a loved one every single day. You can even calendarise care.
core_ideas.quote: I didn't mean transactional, I meant intentional in the sense, not calculative, but caring.

core_ideas.concept: The world is a museum of passion projects
core_ideas.explanation: John Collison notes that every hotel, park and railway exists because someone tenaciously made it happen. Ajay adds a Turkish proverb: a forest takes a hundred years to grow and one night to burn. Frontier economies like the US or Switzerland are centuries-old Rube Goldberg machines, so he shares the conservative instinct to avoid wrecking balls.
core_ideas.quote: I share the conservative view that you know don't bring a wrecking ball to these things. They're very complex. We dimly understand them, and once destroyed, they'll be very hard to recreate.

core_ideas.concept: Talent is mostly born abroad, and migration is positive-sum
core_ideas.explanation: Paul Graham's math means the best teams must be international. Ajay says Indian firms should hire explicitly multinational workforces, as Gukesh did and as university rankings reward through foreign faculty and students. Amit adds that low-skilled migrants do jobs locals won't, and that slums are a city's entry point. High-skilled immigration builds clusters that attract more talent.
core_ideas.quote: If a country has five percent of the world's population and ability is evenly distributed, then 95% of the people who are best at any given thing will be born abroad.

core_ideas.concept: A culture of mavericks fattens the upper tail
core_ideas.explanation: With 1.4 billion people, India has huge numbers of exceptional people, and so wastes many Ramanujans; that is why growth matters ('people are brains, not stomachs'). Ajay argues that variance is cultural as well as biological. A society that embraces dissidents and nonconformists widens its distribution and gets more outliers at the top, where all good things come from. An obedient, straight-laced culture gets a tight distribution.
core_ideas.quote: If you're one in a million remember there are 1400 of you in India because India has 1400 million people.

core_ideas.concept: Imperfectionism, done right
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's mantra, echoing Dharmesh: you suck at anything when you start, so keep a bias for action, ship and iterate. Yet perfection and production aren't opposites. Ajay's caveat: put in the volume, but ship your genuine best each time and pull the general principle out of every piece of feedback.
core_ideas.quote: Because for me, you know, perfection is achieved only through constant production. Production is necessary on the path to perfection.

core_ideas.concept: A tool, not a crutch: think above the API
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's advice to writers asking about Grammarly, Hemingway or ChatGPT applies to mentors too. People who mechanically apply corrections without asking why aren't doing higher-order thinking. They are exactly the people AI will replace, which may spur everyone to get more out of themselves.
core_ideas.quote: by all means use it as a tool, but do not use it as a crutch.

core_ideas.concept: Two stages of procrastination
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's stage one is really marination: he mulls a problem until the pieces click, then writes in a torrent. Stage two is perfectionist terror of the idea that arrives too late. His fix borrows software's bug curve: plot new ideas per day after finishing, and ship once the count has held at zero for a couple of days.
core_ideas.quote: And at this point I've stopped calling it procrastination. I think I was actually thinking.

core_ideas.concept: Thin desires vs thick desires
core_ideas.explanation: Via Luke Burgis and René Girard: thin desires are mimetic, like wanting a Mercedes because someone else has one, wanting to be Arnold, or wanting book prizes and lit-fest stages. Thick desires are intrinsic: loving the dull ache of lifting, or the work of filling a blank page. Ronnie Coleman's line captures the gap. A gym membership you never use is a thin desire.
core_ideas.quote: So I think that this is also something useful to think about, that the people with the thin desire, they won't put in the hard yards.

core_ideas.concept: Outwit the guy in your head, or find a purpose
core_ideas.explanation: Bourdain's life was a series of stratagems to outwit the lazy guy in his head, and Amit's lazy guy is so big he dwarfs him (online chess, YouTube rabbit holes). Ajay has never felt that conflict: he calls himself a junkie who wakes up thirsting for more. His only problem is triage among too many wonderful things.
core_ideas.quote: So I think like find purpose, the rest will follow would be sort of my motto

core_ideas.concept: There's no 'making it', but the real enemy is short-termism
core_ideas.explanation: Sahil Bloom's lion and gazelle must run every day, and Apple must keep making iPhones. Amit warns that good times can get too good and breed complacency. Ajay finds that view too bleak. Most of us have space; the real choke points are playing short-term versus long-term, and chasing likes instead of genuine thought. Workaholics need more risk, not more grind.
core_ideas.quote: I think a lot of EIE viewers are workaholic, but not enough risk is present in their lives and in their worlds.

core_ideas.concept: Your future is constantly shrinking
core_ideas.explanation: Gurwinder Bhogal's call to action, alongside Burkeman's Four Thousand Weeks. Amit suggests an exercise for people in their thirties living away from their parents: optimistically estimate their remaining years and how often you'll visit each year. The total is startlingly small.
core_ideas.quote: Your future is constantly shrinking. So the longer you spend preparing for it, the smaller it's going to be.

core_ideas.concept: You only control you
core_ideas.explanation: When people voice vague angst about the world, Ajay asks: so what are you going to do? Be selfish. You have tomorrow: what will you read, write, do, and who will you meet? Becoming a very good you creates positive externalities for everyone around you. Amit: nothing stands between you and your best version except your actions.
core_ideas.quote: You actually only control one thing which is what do you do. Everything else is outside your control.

core_ideas.concept: Zoom out, then act
core_ideas.explanation: Frog's father promises that spring is around the corner. Sahil Bloom's zoom-out chart shows that daily noise becomes a rising line over decades. Amit adds the catch: things only get better when you do things. Ajay agrees: whether you're crushed under an authoritarian regime in Russia or invaded in Ukraine, you still have to wake up and do things.
core_ideas.quote: Spring does not come on its own. Perhaps spring is already there and you just have to look inside your mind to find it. But your actions also matter

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on excuses: 'William Shakespeare did not say, I don't have a laptop, I'm not gonna write... He found a quill from somewhere, as I presume they used.'

Ajay mocking writers who can't write a great book because they haven't been invited to 'a Rockefeller Foundation castle in Italy' or don't own a hundred-dollar pen. You can sit on the floor of an Indian second-class train and think.

After Ajay says chess is for the young mind, Amit: 'This is a comment on my chess addiction. I am deeply disappointed, Ajay Shah.' He then extends the old line: youth is wasted on the young, and 'wisdom is wasted on the old because what are we gonna do with it?'
Ajay's 'last time' exercise includes 'the last time I will drink hot chocolate with seven hundred grams of sugar'. Amit: 'This could be the last episode we record. Who knows? I mean I hope not.'

Ajay: 'Now I'm very smart... I have a full theory of stage one procrastination. I am comfortable with my stage one procrastination... I think I was actually thinking.' Amit: 'The Bengali word for it is marination.'
Amit on thin desires: buying an annual gym membership, never going, and showing up a year later to protest 'paisa toh diya tha' (but I paid!).
Amit on Bourdain's lazy inner guy: his own is so huge 'he practically dwarfs me... you could say this guy is me and I am subsidiary to him.'

Amit updates Sahil Bloom's savannah: today's lion can store all the gazelles he wants in the freezer, and the gazelle can live in a gated society far from lions. He adds, 'Like no one should be eaten.'

Ajay arrived without his promised seven recommendations, so Amit drafted the crew. 'Two of them are truly beautiful, inside and outside. And you put them behind the camera. The good Lord put the ugly one in front of the camera.'

On Ajay's broken promise to watch one film a month: 'I'll watch movies thoroughly when you turn cartwheels on the floor.' Amit: 'Bro, if I try to turn cartwheels on the floor, I could get another heart attack. You can watch movies without any danger to your health. Kindly consider.'
Their friend Shruti Rajagopalan, a huge John Coltrane fan, named her two dogs Cole and Train.
Jacob Bronowski's The Ascent of Man: Ajay contrasts the old model, where the BBC had to commission such work, with YouTube's democratisation.
Bob Dylan, 'He not busy being born is busy dying', and Annie Dillard, 'how we spend our days is how we spend our lives', both quoted by Amit on comfort zones and greatness.
From Good Gyan 1: if you have to reach beyond the horizon, you have to let the shore go.
Amit reaches for Hindustani words, thehrav and sukoon, for the stillness that lets ideas soak in, saying no English word captures the flavour.
An old Turkish proverb, via Ajay: it takes a hundred years to grow a forest and one night to burn it down. He calls advanced economies Rube Goldberg machines.
Ramanujan: 'just think of all the Ramanujans in India who are being wasted'. Ajay notes the one who was found died early, partly from the privation of his early years.
Ajay dismisses Sahil Bloom's lion-and-gazelle parable as a 'life is short, nasty, and brutish view of the world'.
René Girard's mimetic desire, via Luke Burgis: 'They want a Mercedes, so we must feel, we want a Mercedes too.'
Ajay recalls Roger Waters in The Final Cut looking back at his younger self: 'Does anybody love you? Or is it just a crazy dream?'

Procol Harum's 'A Whiter Shade of Pale', which Amit first heard in Scorsese's Life Lessons (starring Nick Nolte and Rosanna Arquette) over a slow-motion shot of a cigarette falling and bouncing on the ground.
